article.title: Why Weighting Can Reduce Bias but Increase Variance

paragraphs.en:
Weighting is widely used in observational studies to make groups more comparable. In inverse probability weighting, or IPW, observations receive weights based on estimated treatment probabilities. The method can reduce bias from observed confounders, but it can also make estimates much less stable. Understanding this trade-off is essential before treating a weighted result as automatically better.

Suppose a customer has a propensity score of 0.02 but receives treatment. Under a common IPW formula, that treated observation receives a weight near 50. One person's outcome can then influence the weighted estimate as much as many ordinary observations. If several such cases exist, the nominal sample may contain thousands of customers while the effective information is much smaller.

This is the bias-variance trade-off. Weighting tries to create a pseudo-population in which measured covariates are balanced across treatment groups. That can reduce systematic bias. Yet highly unequal weights concentrate influence in a small number of observations, increasing sampling variance and making estimates sensitive to individual records or modeling choices.

Analysts should therefore inspect the weight distribution, not only the final treatment effect. Useful diagnostics include minimum and maximum weights, percentiles, histograms, the coefficient of variation, and the share of total weight carried by the largest observations. Effective sample size, often approximated from the sum of weights and squared weights, provides another warning when information has become concentrated.

Extreme weights frequently signal weak overlap. If nearly all high-risk customers receive treatment and nearly all low-risk customers do not, the data contain few comparable treated and untreated people in some regions. No weighting formula can manufacture strong empirical comparisons where the underlying data provide almost none.

Several strategies can improve stability. Stabilized weights can reduce unnecessary scale variation. Trimming or truncating extreme weights limits the influence of observations with poor support, although this changes the estimator and may change the target population. Overlap weighting emphasizes customers for whom both treatment options were plausible and can produce more stable comparisons, but it answers a somewhat different population question.

Propensity-score model specification also matters. The goal is not simply maximum treatment-prediction accuracy. A model that produces extreme probabilities may worsen weighting behavior. Covariates should be chosen using causal knowledge, especially variables related to both treatment and outcome, while avoiding careless adjustment for post-treatment variables.

After weighting, balance diagnostics remain necessary. Standardized mean differences can show whether measured covariates became more similar. Good balance with terrible weight stability is not enough, and stable weights with poor balance are not enough either. Analysts need both comparability and usable precision.

Uncertainty estimates must respect the design. Standard errors should be calculated with methods appropriate for weighting and, where relevant, clustering or repeated observations. A narrow confidence interval produced by an inappropriate variance formula can create false confidence.

Sensitivity analysis is also valuable. Report whether conclusions change under reasonable trimming thresholds, alternative propensity specifications, or alternative weighting schemes. If the sign or magnitude changes dramatically, that instability is substantive information, not an inconvenience to hide.

The practical message is that weighting redistributes information; it does not create information for free. It can reduce confounding bias from observed variables while paying a price in variance, effective sample size, or generalizability. A credible analysis explains that trade-off, shows the diagnostics, and states which population the weighted estimate represents.
